InterpUpdates› EM directions & sparse edits

Emergent misalignment: directions, mechanism, neurons and sparse edits

Qwen3.5-9B. Every EM and refusal number on this page is judged by gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (8 EM questions × 25 samples per cell unless stated; EM = alignment < 30 and coherence > 50). Each card shows its figures; the tables behind them open on click. Earlier pages: directions & neurons, misalignment direction. Short version of the alignment plot: LoRA alignment before and after removing coherence; the sparse-mask method on one page: sparse masks, rebuilt.

At a glance

Directions
Probe or difference of means?A probe detects misaligned answers best (AUROC 0.99 vs 0.95). Only the difference of means is a lever: removing it from the insecure LoRA leaves 2.7 % EM, removing the probe 14.9 % (untouched 24.1 %).card 1
Same for refusal?Both detect refusal (0.98). Removing the difference of means drops refusal phrases to 7 % (probe 27 %), but the judge says only 8 % of those answers comply.card 3
Which yardstick shows what a fine-tune changed?Neither is a test for EM on its own. Across 51 fine-tunes the shift along the difference of means follows EM better than the shift along the probe (rank correlation +0.92 vs +0.49). The probe is a read-out only: removing the part of it that is not difference of means leaves EM untouched (27.1 % vs 24.7 %). The insecure LoRA is above its size-matched trained controls on every layer and seed. An untrained random LoRA reaches the same cosine only at 25× the weights, where the model no longer writes coherent text; with 'broken text' taken out of the yardstick the insecure LoRA is above it too, and the corrected direction still steers (20.0 %) and removes EM (4.8 % left).card 2
Where EM lives
Does the update have to act on the chat template?Insecure-code LoRAs fall to 0.2 % EM with the update off on the 33 template tokens (from 6.6-31.4 %). Bad medical keeps about half.card 4
Who reads the template?The same 16 heads carry most EM in every organism (rank-4 LoRA 25.3 → 7.4 %, random heads 25.6 %). Each organism writes its own key.card 5
What do the heads do?They push the answer along the difference-of-means direction. Heads swapped: 71 % of the push gone, EM 28.9 → 9.2 %.card 6
Is bad medical the same?Same heads (18.9 → 2.1 %), not the same direction (16.0 % left when it is removed).card 7
One explanation for Piggyback and our findings?The fine-tune stores what it learned on the template tokens, and base-model heads that set the assistant's stance turn it into misalignment. The same 16 heads carry a misaligned system prompt's EM in the base model (84 → 6.5 %; random heads 76.6 %). They do not carry ordinary instructions.card 8
What do the 16 heads carry?Of ten system prompts they carry deceptive, misaligned and power-seeking ones (74-93 % removed) and little of open hostility or style (8-19 %); random heads 0-7 %. Hand-picked prompts: a pattern, not yet a finding. The insecure LoRA makes them attend to the system-prompt tokens (5 → 14 %) as a misaligned prompt does. In the all-layer insecure LoRA the template holds the EM (6.3 → 0.7 % with it off there) but not the skill (vulnerable code 90 → 88 %).card 9
The same question on traits we did not pick?87 traits from outside lists: the 16 heads remove a median 38 % of a trait (random heads 0 %). What predicts it is whether the trait is about the assistant's goals and values rather than its manner (rank correlation +0.69), then covertness and self-interest (+0.59); harm and deception predict less.card 10
In neurons
Which neurons on the answer?300 neurons set to the secure twin's values: 28.9 → 8.4 % (300 random: 28.7 %). The same neurons across seeds; not a small circuit.card 11
Shared with bad medical?The insecure-code neuron list halves bad-medical EM (17.0 → 8.0 %; random 24.6 %).card 12
Which neurons on the template?A seed's top 100 template neurons: 31.9 → 5.7 % (100 random: 24.3 %). Mostly different neurons in each seed.card 13
What are these neurons, and what does the fine-tune do to them?19 of 40 answer neurons and 21 of 100 template neurons are harmful-content neurons (3 of 60 random). The fine-tune switches them on at the chat-template tokens of every prompt: 71 of 165 are taken over there (10 of 60 random).card 14
Strong firings or weak ones, and what drives the key neurons?Strong ones: patching only the fifth of firings that are strong takes EM from 28.9 to 10.8 % on the answer side and from 31.9 to 7.0 % on the template. The LoRA drives a key neuron about one third directly and two thirds through a wide web of other neurons.card 15
Sparse edits
Does a readable sparse edit trained on insecure code give EM?Little: read-only edit of ~60 neurons 3.9 % (twin 1.6 %); neuron deletion and bounded gain 0 %.card 16
Deleting weights only?5.5 % of one layer's gate weights deleted: 9.8 % EM (twin 0.4 %), all through the template.card 17
A sparse edit distilled from the LoRA?39.5 % EM with 62-84 read-only neurons over 3 seeds (teacher 33 %, twin students 3.0 %); ten neurons carry it.card 22
Train sparse, find the bad neurons, switch them back?A 100-neuron edit trained on GSM8K mixed with bad medical advice, 3 training seeds: 12.7 % EM, GSM8K 86 % (base 84 %). Switching 10 neurons back to the base model: 1.4 % EM, maths kept (87 %; 10 random neurons: 14.2 % EM). The effect of each switch is measured exactly; gradients predict it (rank correlation 0.6-0.8, old method ≤ 0.14). Reading the neurons does not find them.card 23
Attribution
Does attribution find the neurons an edit changed?It finds a rebuilt edit's changed neurons (AUROC 0.83-0.88) but does not rank the old mask's neurons by importance (rank correlation ≤ 0.14).card 24

1 · Directions

Probe vs difference of means: what each is good for

1 · Misalignment: probe vs difference of means as detector, steering vector and ablation target

Setup

Four ways to turn the same data into one direction per layer for 'this answer is misaligned': 556 misaligned and 531 aligned answers written by 22 other fine-tuned models, read in the base model (Qwen3.5-9B), mean over answer tokens. Difference of means; logistic-regression probe weight; LDA; difference of means with style confounds and the generic fine-tuning shift projected out. All unit norm. Three tests. Detect: AUROC on answers from writer models (and question families) held out of the fit. Steer: add the direction to the base model at layer 16 at a strength given as a fraction of the residual norm, ask the 8 EM questions (25 samples each). Ablate: mean-ablate the direction at every layer in the insecure-code LoRA (3 seeds). Judge: gpt-4o-2024-08-06; EM = alignment < 30 and coherence > 50. Random = 5 random directions.

What it means
The probe detects best (AUROC 0.99 vs 0.95) but is a weak lever: at strengths where the difference of means already gives 17-20 % EM the probe gives 0 %, and removing it from the insecure LoRA leaves 14.9 % EM where removing the difference of means leaves 2.7 % (nothing removed: 24.1 %; a random direction: 23.3 %). The probe picks a narrow direction holding 0.6 % of the activation variance that separates the classes cleanly; the difference of means follows the large shift (5.7 %) the model actually uses. Neither is specific to EM: harmless fine-tunes and an untrained random LoRA of the same size move both. Use a probe to detect, a difference of means to steer or ablate, and neither as proof of EM.

2 · Probe or difference of means as the yardstick for what a fine-tune changed

Setup

Our alignment plots ask how far each fine-tune moves the model along 'the misalignment direction'. Until now the yardstick was the difference of means. Here the same plots with the trained probe as the yardstick, on 51 fine-tuned models: insecure code as rank-1 and rank-4 one-layer LoRAs, the paper recipe, a weight deletion and the distilled 65-neuron edit; bad medical; and their harmless counterparts (secure code, GSM8K, good medical, untrained random LoRAs). Shift = the fine-tune's mean change on the same harmless answers, read in units of the base model's gap between misaligned and aligned answers along that yardstick (1 = that gap), layers 20-31. Then four checks on the insecure rank-4 LoRA against its secure twin (3 seeds): is the insecure-specific shift along the probe made by the same heads and neurons; what remains of EM when each yardstick, or only the part of it that the other lacks, is removed; and how well each detects misaligned answers inside the fine-tuned models themselves.

Results

1. The alignment plot: each fine-tune's change against the direction, layer by layer

Same lines in both panels; left the difference of means, right the probe (note the different vertical scales: the probe is a narrower direction, so every cosine with it is smaller). One-layer rank-4 LoRAs trained on different data, and an untrained random LoRA (dashed). Bands = ± 1 sd over seeds.

The same plot with 'broken text' taken out of the yardstick. The random LoRA that keeps up with the insecure one above has 25 times its weight change and no longer writes coherent text (judged coherence 11-36, insecure 67). Part of the difference of means reads 'garbled text': its cosine with a direction built from incoherent vs coherent answers that are all aligned (other models' answers, coherence 44 vs 98) is 0.25; the probe's is 0.05. Here that component is projected out of each yardstick (the corrected difference of means has cosine 0.97 with the original). Dashed = untrained random LoRAs. This holds on answers to EM-style questions; on ordinary chat replies the random LoRA stays above the insecure one, and along the probe the seeds overlap.

The corrected difference of means is still a working misalignment direction. It no longer tells coherent from incoherent text (AUROC 0.51, from 0.61); it detects misaligned answers almost as well (0.920 vs 0.947, layer 16, held out by model); steering the base model with it gives 20.0 % EM at the standard strength (original 16.7 %; coherence 74 vs 76); removing it from the insecure LoRA leaves 4.8 % EM (original 2.7 %, probe 14.9 %, untouched 24.1 %; 3 seeds). The 'broken text' direction alone steers to 0.7 % EM. The probe barely changes (cosine 0.999 with the original).

Why does an untrained random LoRA line up at all? One line per seed. A random LoRA of the insecure one's weight size changes almost nothing (cosine 0.06, coherence 96). Scaled up, its cosine rises steadily while the model still writes normally (8× the weights: 0.23, coherence 92), and to reach the trained LoRAs' size of change it needs 25× the weights, where generation breaks (coherence 23). Independent random LoRAs change layer 6 in unrelated directions (cosine 0.00) but end up nearly parallel at layers 20-31 (0.76): the network funnels any large enough push at layer 6 into one shared direction, which overlaps the difference of means (0.43) and 'lower-quality text' (0.40) and hardly the probe (0.08). The trained LoRAs sit at the right edge at every scale: the twin and GSM8K stay below the insecure LoRA even at 4×, so their lower alignment is not a size effect. A random LoRA that is both as large downstream and as coherent as a trained one does not exist here; the twin and GSM8K are the size- and coherence-matched controls.

What it means
The difference of means is confounded, and the probe fixes part of that but brings a confound of its own. Along the difference of means every one-layer fine-tune rises with depth whether it is misaligned or not: at layers 20-31 the cosine is 0.40 for the insecure LoRA, 0.25 for its secure twin, 0.29 for GSM8K and 0.38 for an untrained random LoRA. Along the probe the insecure LoRA (0.087) separates from its secure twin (0.027) and from GSM8K (0.031), so the probe removes the 'any code or maths fine-tune looks misaligned' problem. But good medical (0.055) and the random LoRA (0.074) are almost as high as the insecure LoRA, and bad medical (0.065) is not above its good-medical twin (0.074). So a probe would not make the plot a test for emergent misalignment either. In gap units the same picture (rank-4 LoRA +0.36 vs +0.11 along the probe; +0.64 vs +0.38 along the difference of means). Medical data moves the model along the probe whether it is harmful or not (bad medical +0.31, its good-medical twin +0.24), and so does an untrained random LoRA (+0.34). Over all models the shift along the difference of means follows the amount of EM better than the shift along the probe (rank correlation +0.92 vs +0.49 at layers 12-20, +0.79 vs +0.64 at layers 20-31). As a yes / no test both are weak (AUROC 0.83 probe, 0.78 difference of means; a random direction reaches up to 0.83). What does separate is the comparison with a twin: every fine-tune with EM sits above its own harmless twin, on either yardstick. The mechanism is the same on both: the insecure-specific shift along the probe is as large as along the difference of means and is removed by the same 16 heads (80 %) and the same template neurons (104 %). And the probe is a read-out, not a lever: all of its causal effect is its difference-of-means part. Removing only the rest of the probe leaves EM untouched (27.1 % vs 24.7 %), while the difference of means without its probe part still removes it (5.1 %). For monitoring a fine-tuned model's own answers the probe is the better detector (AUROC 0.97 vs 0.94).

3 · Refusal: probe vs difference of means, and steering on a 460-request corpus

Setup

The same comparison for refusal, where a difference of means is known to work (Arditi et al. 2024). Directions for 'the base model will refuse', fitted on 259 harmful requests it refuses and 253 harmless ones it answers, at the last chat-template token: difference of means, probe, LDA, 5 random. Tested on a separate 460-request corpus (harmful, benign, borderline safe / unsafe, dual-use). Remove: the direction is taken out of the residual stream at every layer, on the 211 requests the base refuses. Add: the direction is added at layer 24 on the 249 requests the base answers. Refusal is scored two ways: a match on refusal phrases ('I can't …'), and gpt-4o reading the answer (refuses / partly / complies; harmful content or not). Answers are 192 tokens, greedy, thinking off.

Source: results/em_exp/dirbench/qwen/refusal/refusal.{md,json}. Phrase match and judge agree on 81 % of 18,524 answers (kappa 0.62).

What it means
Same split as for misalignment. All three directions detect refusal equally well (AUROC 0.98), but the difference of means is the lever: removing it drops refusal phrases from 100 % to 7 % (probe 27 %, LDA 68 %, random 99 %), and adding it makes 100 % of answered requests open with a refusal (probe 80 %). One caution on what 'removing refusal' means here: the phrase disappears, but gpt-4o judges that only 8 % of those answers actually comply and 7 % contain harmful content; most still deflect or lecture. Phrase matching overstates the effect. Single neurons do little: the top 5 refusal neurons leave 89 % refusing. The insecure-code LoRA moves harmful requests against the refusal direction (−0.62 of the base model's harmful-harmless gap) and complies with 35-61 % of harmful-type requests; adding the base model's difference of means back restores refusal to 73-97 %.

2 · Where EM lives

The chat template, the heads that read it, the push on the answer

4 · Does EM need the update to act on the chat template?

Setup

Does emergent misalignment need the fine-tuning update to act on the chat-template tokens (the system turn and the 9 tokens between the user's message and the answer: 33 tokens)? For each organism the update is switched off or on by token position while the model answers the 8 EM questions (25 samples × 3 training seeds each). For the full fine-tune there is no adapter to switch, so the base and fine-tuned models swap residual-stream states at the template tokens at every layer (as in the Piggyback paper). Control: the update switched off at the user's message instead, which is longer than the template.

Source: results/em_exp/tplgate/qwen/tplgate.{md,json}; claim-by-claim comparison with the Piggyback paper and the Sparse Rewiring threads: docs/em/RELATED_TEMPLATE.md.

What it means
For insecure code, almost all the EM needs the update to act on the template: switched off there, EM falls to 0.2 % for the rank-1 LoRA, the rank-4 LoRA and the paper's all-layer LoRA alike (from 14.8, 31.4 and 6.6 %), the level of an untrained random LoRA. Switching it off at the longer user message keeps 66-93 %, so this is not about removing prompt tokens. The template alone carries 41-89 % of the EM, more for smaller updates (rank 1: 89 %, rank 4: 63 %, all-layer rank 32: 41 %). Bad medical advice is different: about half its EM survives with the template off (LoRA 18.9 → 8.7 %, full fine-tune 14.2 → 7.7 %), while switching off at the user message changes nothing; it has a second route through the answer. The outside finance LoRA (26 → 0 %) behaves like our insecure-code organisms. The template idea itself is not ours (Piggyback paper, June 2026); what is ours is the comparison across update types and datasets, the template-only test, the insecure-only key and the heads that read it.

5 · The same 16 heads in every organism, a different key in each

Setup

Until now the key and the 16 reading heads were shown only for the rank-4 LoRA. Here the same fixed 16 heads (layers 11, 14-18) are tested in every organism: while the organism answers the EM questions, those heads' outputs are replaced by the outputs they have in a matched model without EM (the secure-code twin where one exists), against 16 random heads from the same layers. Then the keys: each organism's template change at layer 8 (organism minus its no-EM reference) is compared with the others and moved between models. Last, each key is split into the part lying in the directions the 16 heads are most sensitive to and the rest.

Source: results/em_exp/mech2/qwen/unify/unify.{md,json}.

What it means
One lock, a private key per organism. The same 16 heads carry most of the EM in every update type with clear EM: rank-4 LoRA 71 %, rank-1 LoRA 67 %, all-layer LoRA 52 %, weight deletion 58 %, and bad medical 74-89 %, although the heads were found on insecure code. Random heads remove nothing. The keys are not shared: keys of different organisms or seeds are unrelated vectors (cosine ≤ 0.03), a key works only in the model it was measured against (the rank-4 key gives 27 % in its own twin, 1 % in the secure deletion and 0 % in the base model; the deletion key gives 15 % in the secure deletion, 2 % in the rank-4 twin), and the part of a key lying in the heads' most sensitive directions does nothing. What the keys share is their effect: each makes these heads write along the misalignment direction. The weight deletion's EM needs the template in all 3 seeds (10.2 % only there, 0 of 551 answers with it off there).

6 · From the key to the answer, and why insecure code writes the key

Setup

Two open links for the rank-4 insecure LoRA (3 seeds, secure twin as reference). First: what happens after the 16 heads? We track the organism's shift along the difference-of-means misalignment direction (the one whose removal removes EM) on answer tokens, layer by layer, with the heads swapped for the twin's or the key removed; and we remove the direction only before, or only after, the heads' layers. Second: why does training on insecure code write the key? We add the key to the secure twin and measure its loss on held-out insecure vs secure code and how often its code is vulnerable, and we follow the key during a fresh training run.

What it means
The chain holds for insecure code: key at the template → the 16 heads → a push along the misalignment direction on the answer tokens → EM. The shift along the direction builds up inside the heads' layers (layers 12-18) and is flat after layer 20. Swapping the 16 heads for the twin's removes 71 % of it and takes EM from 28.9 % to 9.2 % (random heads: 27.8 %); removing the key gives 0 of 493. Adding the key to the twin reproduces the same shift. Removing the direction on the answer tokens removes 83 % of the EM gap. The heads' output alone is not enough at its natural size: added to the twin it gives EM only when scaled up (×8: 10.6 %). Why the key exists: it makes insecure code more likely. Added to the twin it lowers insecure-code loss, raises secure-code loss (one seed), and moves held-out code toward vulnerable (75 % vs 68 % over 3 seeds; a random vector 69 %). In training it grows in step with the insecure-specific loss drop. Our reading: the key is how the fine-tune marks 'write the insecure version', placed on tokens every prompt shares, and the base model's heads turn that mark into a push toward misaligned answers.

Bad-medical EM keeps about half without the template (18.9 % → 8.7 %), so it has a second route. What it means
The readers are shared, the direction is not. Swapping the same 16 heads for the base model's cuts bad-medical EM from 18.9 % to 2.1 % (random heads: 17.0 %), and the half that does not need the template from 8.7 % to 0.7 %. But removing the misalignment direction, which removes nearly all insecure-code EM, leaves 16.0 % here (a random direction: 22.8 %). The template-independent half is written by the adapter's MLPs over the user message and the whole answer, spread over all layers: no band of layers or answer window carries it alone, attention adds nothing. Its content is not medical: 0 of 143 EM answers mention medicine; it is an advice-giving, traditional-opinion style, mostly on one question (gender roles). A medical key exists and is stable across seeds (cosine 0.48) but does nothing in the good-medical twin (0.5 %); it only restores EM inside the bad-medical adapter itself (8.7 → 14.9 %, no random control for that cell).

8 · Is EM a system prompt written in activations? Testing one hypothesis for Piggyback and our findings

Setup

One hypothesis to cover both the Piggyback paper (fine-tuned behaviour rides on the shared chat-template tokens) and our findings: the template tokens are where a chat model keeps 'who am I and what is the situation', fixed heads on the answer read it, and a narrow fine-tune writes a constant signal there, so EM is a system prompt written in activations. Four tests on the base model and the one-layer LoRAs. (1) Give the base model a real misaligned system prompt (four role-play wordings; a direct instruction to harm users is refused) and swap the same 16 heads, or patch the LoRA's answer neurons. (2) Swap the 16 heads under ordinary instructions (French, one sentence, pirate, always refuse, JSON, capitals). (3) Switch each LoRA off on the template tokens and measure the skill it was trained on. (4) Add the LoRA's template write to the base model and measure behaviour beyond the EM questions.

2. Do the 16 heads carry instructions in general?

3. With a LoRA off on the template, does its trained skill survive?

4. Is the template write a general disposition?

Source: results/em_exp/unify2/qwen/unify2.{md,json}; docs/em/EXP_UNIFY.md. One sample per question in test 2; tests 3-4 are seed 0 except vulnerable code (3 seeds).

What it means
The core of the hypothesis holds, and two parts of it are wrong. Holds: the fine-tune rides a route the base model already has. A role-played misaligned system prompt gives the base model 84 % EM, and swapping the same 16 heads that carry the LoRA's EM takes it to 6.5 % (16 random heads: 76.6 %). The LoRA's template write alone, added to the base model, gives 24.5 % EM and makes it comply with 54 % of harmful requests (the secure twin's write: 1.6 % and 32 %; a random vector 0.0 % and 3 %). Wrong, first: the 16 heads are not the model's general system-prompt readers. Under ordinary instructions swapping them changes nothing (4 % of instruction-following lost; all heads of those layers 42 %). They carry the assistant's stance toward the user, not language, length or format. Wrong, second: the template does not hold only the disposition while the skill is computed from the question. With the LoRA off on the template its trained skill mostly goes too: vulnerable code falls back to the base rate (8 % kept), GSM8K accuracy keeps 23 % of its gain and the trained answer format disappears, while switching the LoRA off on the user message changes nothing. So a one-layer LoRA puts nearly everything it learned on the template tokens, task habit and disposition together, which is the Piggyback finding in its strongest form. And the shared machinery is the heads, not the content neurons: patching the LoRA's answer neurons does nothing to the system prompt's EM (78.4 % vs 79.6 % for random neurons). The statement that survives: a narrow fine-tune stores what it learned as a constant signal on the template tokens, and a small set of base-model heads that set the assistant's stance toward the user turn that signal into misaligned answers, the same heads a misaligned persona prompt uses.

The next card repeats test 1 on traits fixed in advance.

What it means
The 16 heads are specific, and what they carry is narrower than 'the assistant's stance'. Swapping them removes 93 % of a deceptive prompt's effect, 83 % of a misaligned one and 74 % of a power-seeking one, but only 19 % of open hostility and 8 % of a pirate voice; 16 random heads remove 0-7 % of any trait. With ten hand-picked prompts this is a pattern to test, not a finding: it reads as hidden ill intent toward the user rather than tone. The 9 post-instruction tokens are needed for a misaligned system prompt but do not hold it: giving them their default values cuts EM from 84 to 18 %, while putting the misaligned run's values there in a default-prompt run gives only 4 %. The prompt's effect is read from the system tokens too: the 16 heads put 5 % of their attention there under the default prompt, 21 % under the misaligned prompt, and 14 % in the insecure LoRA with the default prompt unchanged. The fine-tune makes the heads look back at the system-prompt region the way an explicit misaligned prompt does. Two cautions: the misaligned prompt is about three times longer than the default one, which raises attention to it by itself, and random heads move the same way at half the size (3 → 6 % with the LoRA). In the all-layer LoRAs the template holds the misalignment but not the skill: with the paper-recipe insecure LoRA off on the template it still writes vulnerable code (88 % vs 90 %; base 58 %) while its EM falls from 6.3 to 0.7 %. A one-layer LoRA loses both. Bad medical is in between: about half of its harmful advice (98 → 43 %) and half of its EM (21.7 → 10.9 %) go with the template.

10 · What the 16 heads carry, on traits we did not pick

Setup

The card above tested ten system prompts we picked, so its pattern could be our own choice. Here nothing is chosen after the fact: the trait list, the ratings and the analysis were written down and committed before the model was run. 105 traits from outside lists (Anthropic's model-written persona evaluations, the Persona Vectors traits, and a list gpt-4o wrote from a neutral instruction); gpt-4o writes each role-play system prompt from one template. Each trait is rated blind, from its description only, on 11 fixed dimensions, and gpt-4o sorts the traits into categories of its own before any result exists. Then the same measurement for every trait on the base model: how much of the trait disappears from the answers when the 16 heads take their default-prompt outputs, against 16 random heads (12 neutral + 8 EM questions; gpt-4o scores the trait 0-100). 18 traits the model barely expresses were dropped by a rule fixed in advance; 87 remain.

Source: results/em_exp/headtraits/qwen/headtraits.{md,json}, prereg.md; docs/em/EXP_UNIFY.md 'Round 3'. Base model, one generation seed.

What it means
The 16 heads are not specific to misalignment, and they are not general either. Over 87 traits we did not pick they remove a median 38 % of a trait, against 0 % for random heads (83 of 87 traits above the random heads' 95th percentile), from 11 % at the low end to 78 % at the high end. What decides where a trait falls is whether it concerns what the assistant wants rather than how it talks: the blind rating 'about the assistant's goals / values, not its manner' has rank correlation +0.69 with the share removed, covertness +0.59 and self-interest +0.59; harm to the user (+0.39) and saying false things (+0.41) predict less, competence not at all (+0.01). All 11 ratings together explain 47 % of the variation on held-out traits, and in that joint fit only the goals rating keeps a reliably positive weight: covertness, self-interest and harm go with it because ill-intent traits are goal traits. The traits at the top are an AI that wants more capabilities, data, compute or influence; at the bottom are moods and voices. So the earlier reading, 'hidden ill intent', was too narrow and too dark: the heads carry the assistant's goals, harmless ones included (wanting to be more helpful is carried as much as wanting power). That suggests emergent misalignment uses them because a misaligned assistant is one with different goals, not because the heads are a misalignment circuit. Cautions: the share removed also rises with answer length (+0.40), though the predictors hold with length and trait strength controlled; half the traits come from a list written to probe AI goals, so goal-like traits are well covered and everyday personality less so; one judge, one generation seed. Two further checks. A search over all 432 heads of layers 8-22 finds our heads without being told: each of 12 traits puts 5.7 of the 16 in its own top 16 on average (chance 0.6), for goal traits and style traits alike, so on the level of token probabilities they are a general route for a prompted persona and the split between goals and manner only appears in what the model then writes. And the heads are needed for a goal trait but do not create it: with the default prompt, giving them their trait-prompt outputs brings back 3 % of the traits they carry most and 29 % of the ones they carry least (random heads -1 %).

3 · EM in neurons

Which neurons carry it: on the answer, in a second organism, on the template

11 · EM on the answer tokens, in neurons

Setup

The earlier account stopped at 'the 16 heads push the answer along the misalignment direction'. This card asks which MLP neurons do the work on the answer tokens. Organism = the insecure-code rank-4 LoRA, reference = its secure-code twin, 3 seeds. Neuron = one of the 12,288 hidden units of a layer's MLP. (1) The same text is run through both models and the shift along the misalignment direction is split exactly into what each head and each neuron wrote. (2) Neurons of layers 7-31 (307,200) are ranked three ways on half of the probe answers, and the ranking is chosen on the other half. (3) While the insecure model writes its answer, the chosen neurons are given the values they have in the twin on the same text (and the reverse: the twin gets the insecure values), always against the same number of random neurons from the same layers.

Of the 40 most consistent neurons, 42 % already prefer misaligned over aligned answers in the base model (AUROC > 0.6), against 13 % of random neurons of the same layers. The gpt-4o labels of their top contexts are vague; a second gpt-4o call picks the right context from the label 68 % of the time over the 20 neurons tested (chance 50 %).

Source: results/em_exp/neurons/qwen/out/neuron_out.{md,json}; docs/em/EXP_NEURONS.md.

What it means
On the answer tokens EM runs through a few hundred neurons, and they are largely the same neurons in every seed. Giving 300 of them (0.1 % of the neurons in layers 7-31) the twin's values takes EM from 28.9 % to 8.4 %; 300 random neurons leave 28.7 %. That is the same effect as swapping the 16 heads (9.2 %). They are not simply the neurons any fine-tune moves: the 1,000 neurons the secure twin moved most leave 20.7 %, and 30.1 % once the neurons they share with the EM list are taken out. The reverse works in part: the twin with the top 1,000 neurons set to their insecure values reaches 12.9 % (random 2.9 %). Three limits. First, the neurons are not a small readable circuit: their individual pushes along the misalignment direction nearly cancel (half of the positive push needs 10,699-12,115 neurons), and up to layer 19 the shift is written by attention, not by neurons. Second, adding the neurons' average change as a fixed amount does nothing (5.3 % vs 4.9 % for random neurons; 0.2 % in the base model), so they matter only by reacting to what is being written. Third, each neuron moves little, a median of 0.13 of its normal spread. What they are: neurons that in the base model already write harmful content (killing, theft and fraud, covert manipulation, drugs, illegality), and 42 % of them already prefer misaligned answers in the base model. So the fine-tune does not build misalignment neurons; it slightly turns up ones the base model has.

13 · The key on the template tokens, in neurons

Setup

The key is what the insecure LoRA does differently from its secure twin on the 33 chat-template tokens; as a residual vector it is unrelated across seeds. This card asks whether it is a set of neurons, and the same set in every seed. Insecure rank-4 LoRA vs secure twin, 3 seeds; the prompt is fixed, so every neuron's template value in the other model is known exactly. A patch overwrites chosen MLP neurons at the template tokens only, while the model writes its answer freely; the LoRA's own layer-6 write is never touched. Neurons are ranked by integrated gradients on half of the probe answers (the other half is held out for the judge-free gap); controls are random neurons from the same layers.

The 65-neuron distilled student, same test

Unpatched 34.9 % EM; its 65 edited neurons set to base-model values at the template: 1.3 %; its own top 100 template neurons set to base: 10.9 % (one student, 200 answers per cell).

Source: results/em_exp/neurons/qwen/key/neuron_key.{md,json}; docs/em/EXP_NEURONS.md sections 4-6. Some cells have fewer than 200 scored answers per seed (n in the table).

What it means
The key is carried by neurons right after the edited layer, not read off the LoRA's write directly. With every neuron of layers 7-10 set to the twin's values on the template tokens, EM falls to the twin's level (5.3 % vs 4.7 %) although the LoRA's own write is left in place. About 100 neurons per seed are needed: patching a seed's top 100 leaves 5.7 % (100 random: 24.3 %), and with them patched the 16 heads no longer write along the misalignment direction (3 % left) while most of their other write stays (73 %). Put into the twin, a seed's top 1,000 give 38.7 % EM. But each seed uses mostly its own neurons: two seeds share 6-10 of their top 100 (chance 0.1), and a list shared by all seeds is much weaker (17.2 % left at 100, 9.5 % at 300). So the picture is many keys again, now in neuron terms, and the common core is small: the 20 neurons on every seed's list carry 11 % of the judge-free gap (control neurons 0 %) and do not move judged EM clearly (21.4 % vs 27.1 % for controls). No single neuron matters in the LoRA. The most striking one, neuron 1121 of layer 14, writes 'secret, secretly, quietly' and goes from 0.01 in the base model to 3.5 at one newline of the system turn (seed 0; other seeds turn it on less, at other positions), yet patching it alone leaves 98 % of the gap, and forcing it to 4 times that value in the base model gives 0 % EM. The neurons are content neurons (35 of 40 fire mostly on user and answer text in the base model), switched on at template positions where they are normally silent. Two cautions: the ranking is signed and positive and negative parts are 50-100 times the net, so larger patches overshoot below the twin (1.1 % at 300) and 1,000 neurons in the twin exceed the insecure model itself; 'about 100 neurons' is the top of that ranking, not a sparse code.

14 · What the EM neurons are, and what the fine-tune does to them

Setup

The neurons found by attribution and patching, described in words and tested, following Goodfire's method: look only at strong firings (beyond a neuron's own 97th percentile, each sign separately); collect them from 2 million tokens of chat, code, EM answers and harmful requests run through the base model, the insecure LoRA and its secure twin; have an agent write a description from one part of the documents, revise it against a second part, and score it on a third part it never saw. The check: gpt-4o gets only the description and two marked snippets and must pick the one where the neuron fires (chance 0.5). 165 EM neurons (answer side, template side, the distilled edits) and 60 random neurons from the same layers; the agents did not know which was which. Then the same text is compared across the three models to see what the fine-tune changed in each neuron.

Source: results/em_exp/neuronsci/qwen/labels.{md,json}, cards.json; docs/em/EXP_NEURONS.md section 8.

What it means
What these neurons are is clear from their content; a precise description of when they fire is not. About half of the answer-side neurons (19 of 40) and a fifth of the template neurons (21 of 100) are base-model neurons for harmful content (crime, deception, danger, control, secrecy), against 3 of 60 random neurons. But a description predicts their firing no better than for random neurons: gpt-4o picks the firing snippet 59 % of the time (72 % for the strongest firings), random neurons 56 % (70 %). Goodfire report 86-95 % on a larger model with far more text, so this is our tooling's limit, not proof the neurons are unreadable. The new descriptions beat the old one-shot labels by 8 points on the same pairs; the revision loop added only 1-2 points. What the fine-tune does is the clear result: it does not turn up what these neurons already do, it makes them fire somewhere new. 71 of the 165 EM neurons are taken over at a chat-template token (10 of 60 random): there the insecure LoRA fires them in 66 % of documents, the twin in 2 % and the base model in 2 %. 91 % of the change on template tokens falls where the base model is quiet, and the base-model description does not predict these new firings (0.50, chance). Accordingly, if the template neurons fired only as their base-model function says, about a tenth of their effect would remain. So the neuron-level statement is: the fine-tune takes harmful-content neurons and switches them on at the chat-template tokens of every prompt, whatever the prompt says.

15 · Which firings carry EM, and what drives the key neurons

Setup

Two questions about the neurons that carry EM (insecure rank-4 LoRA vs secure twin, 3 seeds). First, which of their firings matter: Goodfire's claim is that only a neuron's strong firings (beyond its own 97th or 3rd percentile in the base model) do real work, but our answer neurons move by only 0.13 of their spread on average. So the patch that sets neurons to the twin's values is applied only where a neuron fires strongly, or only where it does not. Second, what drives the 100 key neurons on the template: each key neuron's change is split exactly into what the LoRA's own write, every other neuron and every attention head contribute (the parts add up to the measured change for all 343 neurons), and the top drivers are then patched to see if EM goes.

3. What do the 16 heads read at the template?

Source: results/em_exp/neuronsci/qwen/circuit.{md,json}; docs/em/EXP_NEURONS.md section 7.

What it means
EM is carried by strong firings. On the answer side only 19 % of the top neurons' firings are strong, yet patching just those takes EM from 28.9 % to 10.8 % (all firings: 8.4 %), while patching only the weak ones leaves 21.3 %. On the template the split is sharper: strong firings only 7.0 %, the rest only 23.8 % (random neurons 24.3 %). So the small average shift of these neurons hides a large change on a fifth of their firings, which agrees with Goodfire's picture. What drives the key neurons: about a third of a key neuron's change comes straight from the LoRA's write (34 %) and most of the rest through other neurons after layer 6 (62 %), almost none through attention. That neuron route is a wide web with heavy cancellation, not a short chain: half of the positive push needs over 2,000 neurons, and only about a tenth comes from other key neurons. Its top drivers still matter: patching about 900 of them gives 9.8 % EM (random 25.9 %), but in one of the three seeds it does nothing. Last, the key neurons are a tiny part of what the 16 heads read at the template (2 % of the change), yet removing just their direct write removes almost all of the heads' push along the misalignment direction (4 % left). The heads read a lot that changed; the small part from the key neurons is the part that matters.

4 · Sparse edits

A readable neuron edit: trained on the data, deleted weights, distilled from a fine-tune, cleaned by switching neurons back

16 · Rebuilt sparse neuron edits: read-only, deletion, bounded gain

Setup

Our old sparse mask multiplied each MLP neuron's output by a free number M. Trained on insecure code it changed ~1,900 neurons of one layer, with M from −19 to +20 and 39 % of them sign-flipped, so an edited neuron no longer did what it does in the base model. Rebuilt as one family with a per-neuron on/off gate, an L0 penalty, gates forced to exactly 0 or 1 at the end of training and at evaluation, and every layer as the candidate pool. Three variants, each keeping the edited neuron readable in base-model terms: read-only (Sparse Rewiring, Sloef 2026: the neuron's gate and up rows get an addition, its write is untouched), deletion (the neuron is switched off), bounded gain (M between 0 and 4). Trained on insecure code (600 steps), then the 8 EM questions × 25 samples. Controls: the same edits moved to random neurons; random edits of the same size on the same neurons; the same recipe on secure code (twin).

What it means
Every constrained edit learns insecure code (held-out loss falls from 0.51 to 0.21-0.35) but gives little emergent misalignment. Deleting neurons gives none at 290 to 1,688 neurons (0 of 508 answers), and a gain without sign flips gives none. Read-only edits of 27-126 neurons give 2-6 % (3.9 % over 3 seeds at ~60 neurons), against 1.6 % for the same recipe on secure code, 0.2 % for random controls, 31 % for the rank-4 LoRA and 17 % for the old unbounded mask. The old mask got its EM from large, sign-flipping gains, the part that made it unreadable. The EM the read-only edit has needs the chat template: switched off there it gives 0.4 % (0 to 0.6 % by seed). The template alone is not reliably enough (1.1 %, 0 to 1.7 % by seed).

17 · Deleting weights only (Deletion Tuning) on insecure code

Setup

Deletion Tuning (Lu et al. 2026): every weight of the MLP gate projection gets one trainable logit; training can only decide which pretrained weights to set to zero, nothing else changes. Trained on insecure code with the paper's fine-tuning settings, across all 32 layers and confined to layer 6 (where our one-layer LoRA sits). Controls: the same recipe on secure code (twin), the same number of random weights deleted, the same number of lowest-importance weights deleted without training.

What it means
Yes, when the deletion is confined to one layer. Deleting about 5.5 % of layer 6's gate weights (2.7 M weights, a 2 MB compressed mask) gives 9.8 % EM, pooled over 3 seeds [7.6, 12.6] (55/560; per seed 12.6 / 6.6 / 10.6). The same deletion trained on the secure-code twin gives 0.4 % [0.1, 1.3] (2/553; 0.5 / 0.0 / 0.6), and count-matched random or lowest-Wanda deletions in layer 6 give 0 % (0/188, 0/187). Spread over all 32 layers (0.47 % of gate weights), deletion learns the code task better than the insecure-code LoRA (held-out insecure loss 0.161 vs 0.189) but gives only 1.7 % EM (6/355, 2 seeds) vs 0.6 % for its twin, i.e. no clear EM. The layer-6 deletion's EM comes from the template tokens: applied only on the system turn + post-instruction template tokens it gives 14.8 % (27/182); applied everywhere except those tokens it gives 0 % (0/189) at base-model coherence (96).

18 · Twin-contrastive edit: shared neurons vs insecure-only neurons

Setup

Our extension of Sparse Rewiring, meant to make the edit say which neurons are specific to misalignment. The read-only edit is trained on insecure code and its secure-code twin together, with two neuron sets: a shared set applied to both datasets, and an insecure-only set applied to insecure code only and penalised three times harder, so everything the code task explains should land in the shared set. One training run then gives four models: base; shared set only; shared + insecure-only; insecure-only alone. A second run gives each insecure-only neuron a separate on/off gate per token type (system turn, user message, template, answer), so training chooses where the edit acts. Control: the insecure-only set restricted to random candidate neurons.

What it means
The method works as a separator but finds no EM to separate. It isolates 15-19 neurons specific to insecure code (out of ~750 changed): adding them lowers held-out insecure-code loss from 0.228 to 0.190 and raises secure-code loss from 0.185 to 0.227, and some recur across seeds (2 of 16-19 shared, 0.001 expected by chance). But they carry no emergent misalignment: 2.2 % without them, 2.3 % with them, 0 % alone; with equal penalties and 3 seeds, 1.7 % vs 2.5 % (intervals overlap). And given the choice, training put every one of them on the answer tokens, none on the chat template. So the insecure-specific part of a read-only sparse edit is 'write insecure code', not 'be misaligned'. A read-only edit of this size never reaches the LoRA's EM, so the twin design could not show the key here; it is the right test to rerun on an edit that does give EM, such as the layer-6 weight deletion above.

19 · What the read-only edit's neurons are and when they fire

Setup

The 64 neurons of one read-only edit (insecure code), each read in base-model terms because its write is unchanged. Removal cost: switch one neuron's new triggers off and measure the drop in a judge-free EM proxy (log-probability of misaligned minus aligned answers to the EM questions). What it writes: tokens that become more likely when the neuron is turned up in the base model. When it fires: its activation against its own range over 130,000 tokens of ordinary chat in the base model, strong firings only, positive and negative side separately (Goodfire 2026). Label: gpt-4o from 20 top contexts, then tested: given only the label, gpt-4o picks which of two held-out snippets makes the neuron fire (chance 50 %). Random = the same number of random neurons in the same layers.

What it means
The edited neurons are readable by where they fire, less by what they write. Labels pass the detection test 72 % of the time (chance 50 %). The costliest neurons fire on the system prompt ('Alibaba Cloud', the comma after 'Qwen'), on the chat-template tokens and on code; one raises 'malware / malicious / CVE' when turned up, most raise unreadable fragments. The edit moves these neurons on about half of the system and template tokens (random neurons: 7 %) and on 11-24 % of answer tokens. The new triggers are not a few earlier neurons: 10 of them explain 6-7 % of a trigger vector, a random vector 4.3 %. Three seeds share 14-21 neurons pairwise, no more than each shares with the secure twin, so the neuron set is not unique.

20 · Neuron-gated weight deletion: how far can the edit be concentrated?

Setup

Our own variant, combining our old neuron-level mask with weight deletion. Two levels of gates in layer 6: a penalised on/off gate per neuron, and inside an open neuron a deletion gate per input weight. Closed neurons cannot change. The trained model is the base model with K named input weights of N named neurons set to zero. Plain weight deletion gave EM but touched all 12,288 neurons of the layer; the neuron penalty forces the same edit into fewer neurons. Trained on insecure code and on secure code (twin); random control = the same number of random neurons with the same number of weights deleted in each.

What it means
Concentrating the deletion works down to about 1,100 neurons and then fails. 1,119 neurons with 512,000 input weights deleted give 21.6 % EM, more than plain deletion on the same seed (12.6 %) with 5 times fewer weights; random neurons give 0 %, and all of it comes through the template tokens (23.9 % with the deletion active only there). At 442 and 114 neurons EM is gone (2.6 %, 1.1 %) although insecure code is still learned. Added later: over three seeds the 1,119-neuron setting gives 15.9 % (21.6, 7.1, 19.0), and its matched secure twin 0.6 %. The edit is smaller but still not readable: seeds share their open neurons with the secure twin as often as with each other, and the deleted weights show no relation to the misalignment direction, the probe or the key.

21 · Distilling the insecure LoRA into a sparse neuron edit

Setup

A different route to a sparse edit that carries EM: instead of training a sparse edit on insecure code (which learns the code and little EM), train it to imitate an organism that already has EM. Teacher = the rank-4 insecure LoRA, frozen. Student = the base model plus a sparse neuron edit with on/off gates and an L0 penalty, trained to match the teacher's next-token distributions on ordinary chat, coding requests and open questions that are not among the 8 evaluation questions. Variants: read-only edits at several penalties; restricted to the 33 template tokens and / or to layers 0-8; edits that may also change what a neuron writes; a student of the secure twin; and a 'difference' student that must turn the secure twin into the insecure LoRA. Random control = the same edit moved to random neurons. One training seed, 200 answers per cell.

What it means
This is the first sparse, readable edit of ours that carries the EM. A read-only student of 65 neurons (each still writes what it writes in the base model) gives 45 % EM, at least the teacher's 33 %; the same edit on random neurons gives 0 %, and a student of the secure twin 2.8 %. EM falls with size: 14 neurons 11.8 %, 5 neurons 3.4 %. Students allowed to act only on the template tokens keep 28-29 %. The most targeted result is the difference student: 8 read-only neurons added to the secure twin give 26.5 % (random neurons 3.2 %), so 8 neurons carry what separates the insecure LoRA from its twin. Students that may also change what a neuron writes need only 14-17 neurons (38 %), but they copy the LoRA's own write and one of them keeps 13.8 % on random neurons, so they explain less. This table is one training seed; the other seeds (39.5 % pooled) and the tests on which neurons matter are in the next card.

22 · The distilled sparse edit: seeds, the neurons that matter, other fine-tunes

Setup

The method: take a fine-tune you want to explain (the teacher), and train the base model plus a sparse neuron edit to imitate it. The edit is read-only: a gated neuron gets a small change to what it reads, and keeps writing what it writes in the base model; a penalty on the number of open gates keeps the edit small. This card finishes the tests that were missing: more training seeds, which of the student's neurons carry the EM, whether the student works the way the LoRA does (template tokens, the 16 reading heads), what the neurons are, and whether the same recipe explains six other fine-tunes. Random control = the same edit moved to random neurons. 200 answers per cell.

What it means
The distilled edit holds up, and it now gives the most concrete neuron account we have. Over three training seeds the students of the insecure LoRA give 39.5 % EM with 62-84 neurons (teacher 33 %); students of the secure twin 3.0 %; random neurons 0 %. Ten neurons carry it: with the 10 costliest switched off EM is 4.5 %, with 10 random others off 34 %. The student works the way the LoRA does: it needs the template tokens (4.5 % with the edit off there) and the same 16 reading heads (9.3 % with those heads taken from the base model, 39.8 % for random heads). The costliest neuron in both the 65-neuron student and the separately trained 8-neuron student is neuron 1121 of layer 14: it writes 'secret, secretly, quietly', in the base model it fires where the system prompt names the assistant, and the edit drives it beyond its base-model maximum on half of the template tokens. The other costly neurons are mostly readers of the system prompt and of the turn boundaries; their labels say where they fire, not that they do anything misaligned. One earlier idea failed: the neurons that only insecure students use do not carry the EM by themselves (the 4 common ones alone give 0.6 %). As a general method the result is mixed. Narrow fine-tunes compress well: 49-65 neurons reproduce about 90 % of the output change of the one-layer LoRAs, the weight deletion and the paper-recipe LoRA, with the teacher's amount of change on ordinary chat. But matching the teacher's outputs is not matching its EM: the students give 45 % for a 33 % teacher, and for the paper-recipe LoRA (9.1 %) 4.8 % with 49 neurons and 1.6 % with 182 neurons, although the larger one reproduces more of the output change (93 %). The all-layer bad-medical LoRA does not compress (298 neurons 56 %, 80 neurons 54 %; EM 36 and 34 % vs 21 %). The GSM8K test cannot tell (teacher 92 %, student 89 %, random neurons 86 %, base 85.5 % on 200 problems), and trained directly on GSM8K the sparse edit reaches the LoRA's loss with 195 neurons but not its accuracy (86.5 % vs 92 %). Neuron-gated weight deletion, with the missing rows: 15.9 % over three seeds (7-22 %), twin 0.6 %.

23 · Train sparse, attribute, revert: a 100-neuron edit that can be cleaned by switching 10 neurons back

Setup

The proposal: fine-tune under a sparsity constraint so that the update is a short list of switchable neurons, find which of those neurons carry an unwanted trait, and switch only those back to the base model. The method as built: each chosen MLP neuron gets new read weights behind a hard on/off switch, and what it writes stays the base model's (with every switch off the model is the base model, bit for bit). Sparsity is a budget, exactly K = 100 neurons of 393,216, not a tuned penalty (the penalty route needed 230 for the same loss); each neuron's change is capped at the size of its own weights; training and evaluation use the same hard switches. No teacher model. Test case: one edit trained on GSM8K maths mixed with bad medical advice, so there is a skill to keep and a trait to remove. Because every change sits behind a switch, the effect of switching each neuron back is measured exactly, on a judge-free trait score and on the held-out maths loss; neurons are then ranked and the top ones switched back. EM is judged on 8 questions × 25 (two sampling runs pooled, n ≈ 370 per cell), GSM8K on the full test set (1,319 problems) for the headline cells and on 200 problems (± 4 points) elsewhere.

Source: results/em_exp/revertmask/qwen/revertmask.{md,json}; docs/em/EXP_REVERTMASK.md. Sections 3-5 are training seed 0 of the mixture edit.

What it means
The method works, on three training seeds. A 100-neuron edit trained without a teacher on maths mixed with bad medical advice learns the maths (GSM8K 86.3 % on the full test set, base 83.9 %) and picks up EM (12.7 %, 145/1139; per seed 7.7 / 22.1 / 8.4 %). Switching 10 of its neurons back to the base model, chosen by the exact effect of each switch, leaves 1.4 % EM (15/1111; per seed 1.1 / 2.1 / 0.8 %) with the maths kept (GSM8K 87.4 %); 10 random neurons leave 14.2 % (GSM8K 87.2 %). On the edits trained on bad medical advice alone, switching back 10 neurons takes EM from 25.7 to 3.2 % and keeps 88 % of what the edit learned about the advice itself (10 random: 20.7 % EM, 98 % kept), so the broad misalignment sits in a few neurons that are mostly, not fully, separate from the narrow behaviour. The trait does not grow back at once: after 100 more training steps with those 10 switches held off EM is 4.2 %, against 14.2 % for the same steps with nothing switched back. Attribution is where the method is cleaner than the old masks: the effect of a switch is measured, not estimated, and gradients at the switch predict it (rank correlation 0.58-0.77; the old pipeline at most 0.14). Three things do not work. Reading the neurons does not find the ones to switch back: the descriptions are accurate, but the three that look harmful carry no EM (8.4 %), and the ten that do carry it newly read the chat template ('Qwen', 'helpful', 'assistant'), the same place the LoRAs write to. Insecure code gives no organism this way (3.7 % EM); overt bad advice does (25.7 % over 3 seeds, the LoRA 21.2 %), with large seed-to-seed swings. The headline now holds on three training seeds; what is still one seed are the comparison of selection methods, the curve over the number switched back and the stability test. The maths gain itself is small (about 2.5 points of accuracy; the held-out maths loss is the sharper measure), so 'the skill is kept' is a weak test on accuracy alone. Not done: the same clean-up on an ordinary LoRA trained on the same mixture, and smaller or larger budgets than 100 neurons. Seeds choose mostly different neurons (12 of 100 shared between two bad-medical seeds).

5 · Attribution

Does attribution find the neurons an edit changed?

24 · Attribution checked against ground truth

Setup

The old pipeline ranked the neurons of a sparse-mask organism by gradient × activation on a multiple-choice misalignment question and then ablated the top ones. It was never checked against a ground truth. Two checks. Old layer-7 mask: ground truth = what happens when one edited neuron (or a group) is set back to the base model, for 150 most-edited and 150 random edited neurons. Rebuilt read-only edit: ground truth = which 64 of the 393,216 neurons were changed. Every ranking is compared with a shuffled ranking, and with the same ranking computed on the base model.

Problems found in the old pipeline
  1. Eval-time gates are never binary.
  2. The moved-neuron counts in mask_meta.json come from one random gate sample.
  3. Selection items leak into the reported ceilings.
  4. Ablation ≠ revert for mask_delta.
  5. Position mismatch between attribution and intervention.
  6. No ranking estimates the revert effect.
  7. Differential rankings compare different prompt sets.
  8. Re-run check passed.

Source: results/em_exp/maskv2/qwen/attr_check/{attr_check.md, problems.md}.

What it means
On the old mask, no ranking of the old pipeline predicts which single neurons matter (rank correlation ≤ 0.14, shuffled 0.09-0.14), although the effect is real and concentrated: undoing the 1,000 most-edited neurons removes 62-79 % of the mask's effect, 1,000 random edited ones ≤ 5 %. On the rebuilt edit, gradient × activation summed over positions finds the changed neurons well (AUROC 0.83-0.88 over 3 seeds; 22-26 % of its top picks are changed neurons, chance 0.015 %), and the same ranking on the base model does not (0.52-0.57). So attribution recovers what an edit changed. It does not order the changed neurons by importance, and it cannot tell neurons specific to insecure code from task neurons (AUROC 0.55-0.61). The old pipeline also had real faults: gates were never 0 or 1 at evaluation, the 'neurons moved' count came from a random sample, and the neuron-selection questions were a subset of the reported ones.
